title: Digital Pathology Market Size, Share & Forecast 2026-2032

market_overview.summary: Digital pathology is the digitisation of glass microscope slides and the software that views, stores and analyses the resulting whole-slide images. It is unusual among healthcare IT markets in being bounded by two exactly countable public registers: the FDA has granted 23 authorisations under product code PSY, the whole slide imaging system regulation at 21 CFR 864.3700, and 46 across the whole digital pathology regulatory family, of which three are de novo classifications; and CMS counts 33,955 non-waived CLIA laboratories, of which it identifies 13,582 as having the institutional profile to digitise. We publish $2,010M for 2026 rising to $3,541.46M by 2032 at 9.90%. Normalised to a common 2026 base, eleven publishers covering the digitisation stack give $714M to $2,010M, a 2.815x spread, while their growth rates run 7.99% to 18.56%, a 2.323x spread. The ratio of those two spreads is 1.21, which means this literature disagrees about size and about growth by almost exactly the same multiple and converges on neither. Dividing the published market through the register settles what no published forecast in this market funds: a complete installed base.
key_trends: The regulatory bottleneck broke in 2024, not gradually. Across the whole life of the whole slide imaging regulation the FDA granted 8 authorisations in the seven years 2017 through 2023 and 15 in the under three years since, with 9 of the 23 total falling in calendar 2024 alone. There were none at all in 2018 or 2020.

Supply is extremely concentrated. Ten companies hold all 23 PSY authorisations and Philips holds 8 of them; there are 590 CMS-identified digital-capable CLIA laboratories for every authorisation ever granted and 1,358 for every company that holds one.

The reimbursement driver pays nothing. The thirteen digital pathology add-on codes 0751T through 0763T are Category III codes with no assigned payment amount, and a Federal Register full-text search run on 18 October 2026 returns zero documents containing 0751T, 0753T or 0763T in the publication's entire history.

AI is now a separate regulated class rather than a feature. Sixteen of the 46 authorisations are software: 14 image viewing and management clearances under 864.3700 and 2 algorithm clearances under 864.3750, with a further three prognosis algorithms under 864.3755, a regulation that did not exist before 2025.

The regulator is moving on access, not on payment. CMS's October 2026 CLIA proposed rule would add digital images and digital data to the records laboratories must store, revise the 5-year cytology and 10-year histopathology slide retention rules, and permit off-site review of images under a defined virtual access regime.

Nobody who sells into this market reports it. Philips holds a third of all whole slide imaging authorisations and discloses no digital pathology revenue; Danaher reports Diagnostics at $9,941M without breaking out Leica Biosystems; only Roche discloses a pathology line at all, and that line is anatomic pathology entire.
market_overview.adoption_level: Partial and institutionally concentrated; CMS's own assumed digital adoption rate in cytology is 25%

drivers: An authorised device base that finally exists. Twenty-three whole slide imaging authorisations from ten companies, 15 of them granted since the start of 2024, means a laboratory choosing a platform in 2026 has a real shortlist for the first time, where between 2017 and 2023 it had one or two.

Regulatory permission to move the image rather than the pathologist. CMS's October 2026 CLIA proposed rule defines virtual access as test analysis, transmission of results, images or data over a secure connection, review at a secure location and transmission back to the primary testing laboratory, which is the legal predicate for remote sign-out.

Workforce scarcity in exactly the segment with the most laboratories. CMS states that approximately 20 percent of all Certificate of Compliance laboratories are in dermatology offices and frames its personnel proposals around access to specialised dermatologic care in rural areas, which is the demand case for telepathology stated by the regulator rather than by a vendor.

A new and separately regulated algorithm class. The three prognosis algorithms authorised under 21 CFR 864.3755 since July 2025, and the two assistive algorithms under 864.3750, create a reimbursable clinical claim that scanning alone never had, because they produce a result rather than a picture.

Proficiency testing is being rewritten around digital images. CMS proposes to allow digital images in gynecologic cytology proficiency testing explicitly to align with FDA-authorised digital cytology screening systems, which removes a standing compliance reason for a cytology laboratory to keep glass.

Instrument vendors are growing the layer underneath. Roche's Pathology Lab customer area grew 14% at constant exchange rates in 2025 to CHF 1,723M, the fastest-growing customer area in its Diagnostics Division, and digitisation attaches to that installed base rather than creating its own.
restraints: The arithmetic does not fund the installed base. Equipping the 13,582 CLIA laboratories CMS itself identifies as digital-capable, at the $1,500,000 top of CMS's own stated whole slide instrumentation range, costs $20,373M, which is 1.072 times the entire cumulative global market 2026-2032 on the forecast we publish.

The add-on CPT codes carry no payment. Category III codes have no relative value units; whatever is paid is paid at a Medicare Administrative Contractor's discretion with no published rate, and the codes may not be reported for AI training or validation, which is the fastest-growing use of digitised slides.

Capital cost per laboratory dwarfs annual market value per laboratory. The whole global market divided across those 13,582 laboratories is $147,990 a year against CMS's $100,000 to $1,500,000 for one scanner, so the ratio of annual revenue to one unit of capital cost is between 1.48x and 0.10x.

The denominator is not growing. Non-waived CLIA laboratories have been flat at 33,000 to 34,000 for five years: 33,033 on a July 2021 QIES snapshot, 33,747 in the December 2023 CLIA fees rule and 33,955 on the August 2025 QCOR pull. Adoption has to come from penetration, not from new laboratories.

Digitisation is an added cost on a service whose payment is under review. CPT 88305, the Level IV surgical pathology code to which the 0753T add-on attaches, is a Physician Fee Schedule service whose valuation CMS has put back out for comment, and the add-on adds no revenue to it.

The literature itself is a commercial obstacle. The same year supports $714M, $2,010M and $11,818M for nominally the same market, a 16.55x range, so a buyer sizing an opportunity from the wrong publisher is wrong by more than an order of magnitude before any execution risk.
opportunities: Replacement and expansion inside the installed base rather than greenfield adoption. Eight of the 23 PSY authorisations are successive submissions from one applicant, which is what a maintained platform looks like, and the 2026 clearances are second and third generation scanners rather than first entries.

Cytology, which the regulator is opening deliberately. CMS counts 3,229 laboratories certified in the cytology subspecialty and assumes about 25 percent of them already use digital images as the primary screening method, which is the only published adoption rate in this market traceable to a government source.

Prognosis algorithms under 21 CFR 864.3755, a regulation created in July 2025 and holding three authorisations. Unlike a scanner, an algorithm that returns a prognostic score has a clinical claim that can carry its own code rather than an unpaid add-on to someone else's.

Image quality control as a separate product. The single authorisation under product code SIX, granted in August 2026, establishes artifact detection software as its own regulated device, which is the kind of unglamorous layer a high-volume digital laboratory has to buy once it stops looking at glass.

Dermatopathology and independent laboratories, the two segments with both volume and distributed sites. CMS's own framing of the personnel proposals around dermatology offices and rural access identifies where remote review has a reason beyond efficiency.

Veterinary pathology, which four of the eleven publishers segment separately and which carries none of the CLIA certification, proficiency testing or Medicare reimbursement constraints that bound the human market.
challenges: Share in this market cannot be computed from any public document. Philips holds 8 of 23 whole slide imaging authorisations and reports no digital pathology revenue; Danaher reports Diagnostics at $9,941M and does not break out Leica Biosystems; Roche reports Pathology Lab at CHF 1,723M, which is anatomic pathology entire and not digital pathology.

The digital pathology and computational pathology literatures collide rather than nest. Five publishers size computational pathology at $715M to $1,871M for 2026, which overlaps the eleven-publisher digitisation stack range of $714M to $2,010M, and Grand View's own two reports imply algorithms are 48.8% of the whole stack.
Regional estimates disagree by more than the thing they divide. North America is 36.74%, 39.92%, 41% and 47.8% of the same nominal market in the same year by four publishers, a 1.30x disagreement.

Product splits contradict each other outright. Software is 42.88% of the market for one publisher while hardware is 58.10% for another and scanners alone are 43.5% for a third, so there is no agreed answer to whether this is a hardware or a software market.

The regulator does not know the installed base and says so. CMS states in print that it is unable to determine how many laboratories have adopted digital images for screening as the primary method of patient testing, and its 25 percent figure is explicitly an assumption.

competitive_landscape.market_position: Holder of the founding de novo and of more whole slide imaging authorisations than any other company; revenue not disclosed
competitive_landscape.description: Philips holds DEN160056, the de novo granted on 12 April 2017 that created 21 CFR 864.3700 and product code PSY, and 8 of the 23 authorisations under that code: K172174 (2017), K192259 (2019), K203845 (2021), K233204 and K241871 and K242848 (2024) and K243871 (2025), across the IntelliSite Pathology Solution and version 5.1. That is a third of the entire authorised universe. Philips reports Diagnosis & Treatment segment sales of EUR 8,531M for 2025 against EUR 8,790M in 2024, with full-year comparable sales growth of 0% and an Adjusted EBITA margin of 11.7%, and discloses no IntelliSite or digital pathology revenue line anywhere in that disclosure. No revenue market share is publicly disclosed.

competitive_landscape.market_position: Second-largest holder of scanner-platform authorisations and the only holder of an image quality control clearance; revenue not disclosed
competitive_landscape.description: Leica Biosystems Imaging holds three PSY authorisations - K190332 for the Aperio AT2 DX System in May 2019, K232202 for the Aperio GT 450 DX in April 2024 and K253554 covering both the Aperio GT 450 DX and the GT 180 DX in August 2026 - and K253561, the single authorisation under product code SIX for the Aperio iQC DX artifact detection software, which makes it the only company holding a digital pathology image quality device. Danaher reported Diagnostics segment sales of $9,941M and operating profit of $2,650M for 2025 against $9,787M and $2,625M in 2024, on total company sales of $24,568M. Leica Biosystems is not reported separately and digital pathology is not reported at all. For scale, the Diagnostics segment alone is 4.95 times the entire global digital pathology market as we size it. No revenue market share is publicly disclosed.

competitive_landscape.market_position: The only participant that discloses a pathology revenue line, and that line is larger than the whole published digital pathology market
competitive_landscape.description: Ventana Medical Systems holds two PSY authorisations, K232879 for Roche Digital Pathology Dx (VENTANA DP 200) in June 2024 and K242783 in December 2024. Roche reports Pathology Lab as a Diagnostics Division customer area: CHF 1,723M in 2025 against CHF 1,599M in 2024, up 14% at constant exchange rates and 8% in Swiss francs, the fastest-growing customer area in a division whose total was CHF 13,847M. At the IRS yearly average rate of CHF 0.831 per dollar for 2025 that is $2,073.4M, or 1.032 times the entire global digital pathology market for 2026 as we size it and 2.904 times the lowest published estimate. The line is anatomic pathology entire - stainers, antibodies, probes, consumables and service - not digital pathology, and Roche restated its 2024 comparatives to move CINtec sales into it, so the growth rate is not comparable with earlier reports. It is cited here because it establishes the scale of the business the digitisation layer attaches to. No digital pathology revenue and no market share is publicly disclosed.

competitive_landscape.market_position: Third-largest holder of whole slide imaging authorisations and the most active applicant of 2026; revenue not disclosed
competitive_landscape.description: Hamamatsu holds four PSY authorisations: K213883 for the NanoZoomer S360MD in September 2022, K233027 in December 2023, K253606 covering the NanoZoomer S20MD and S360MD in July 2026 and K260964 for the NanoZoomer S540MD in July 2026. Two of its four were granted within eight days of each other, which is what a platform refresh looks like in this register rather than a new entry. Hamamatsu publishes no digital pathology or whole slide imaging revenue line. No revenue market share is publicly disclosed.

competitive_landscape.company: Proscia, Sectra, Indica Labs, Shandon Diagnostics and Virasoft
competitive_landscape.headquarters: Philadelphia (United States), Linkoping (Sweden), Albuquerque (United States), Runcorn (United Kingdom) and New York (United States)
competitive_landscape.market_position: One PSY authorisation each; the long tail of the whole slide imaging register
competitive_landscape.description: Five companies hold a single PSY authorisation apiece: Proscia's Concentriq Dx (K230839, February 2024), Sectra's Digital Pathology Module version 3.3 (K232208, April 2024), Indica Labs' HALO AP Dx (K232833, May 2024), Shandon Diagnostics' E1000 Dx Digital Pathology Solution (K241717, February 2025) and Virasoft's Virasight (K251952, July 2026). Several also hold clearances under product code QKQ for image viewing and management software, where Proscia (K261380, Concentriq AP-Dx), Sectra (K193054) and Indica Labs (K252762) all appear. Four of the five entered the register in 2024 or later, which is the clearest single sign that the 2024 step-change was new entrants rather than incumbents refreshing. competitive_landscape.headquarters: New York (United States), Boston (United States), Tel Aviv (Israel) and Los Altos (United States)

competitive_landscape.description: Paige.AI holds DEN200080, the de novo for Paige Prostate granted on 21 September 2021 that created 21 CFR 864.3750, plus two FullFocus clearances under QKQ (K201005, K241273). Ibex Medical Analytics holds the only subsequent 864.3750 clearance, K241232 for Galen Second Read in January 2025. PathAI holds two QKQ clearances, Novo (K212361) and AISight Dx (K243391). Artera holds DEN240068 for ArteraAI Prostate, the July 2025 de novo that created 21 CFR 864.3755, and K254115 for ArteraAI Breast; SimBioSys holds the third authorisation under that regulation, K260023 for TumorSight Risk in September 2026. The whole algorithm tier is therefore 2 clearances under 864.3750 and 3 under 864.3755. None of these companies publishes revenue, and the Category III add-on codes explicitly may not be reported for AI training or validation. No revenue market share is publicly disclosed.

competitive_landscape.company: Barco N.V., Eizo Corporation and Shenzhen Beacon Display Technology
competitive_landscape.market_position: The display layer, three authorisations in nine years; revenue not disclosed
competitive_landscape.description: Product code PZZ, digital pathology display, holds three clearances in total: Barco's MMPC-4127F1 (K172922, December 2017), Shenzhen Beacon Display's 8MP colour LCD displays C811W, C811WT, PA27 and PA27T (K233119, December 2024) and Eizo's RadiForce MX317W-PA (K242545, May 2025). Barco also holds a PSY authorisation, K203364 for the MDPC-8127 in April 2021. The display layer is included because it is the part of the stack a laboratory cannot substitute with existing hardware and is the smallest regulated category in the whole family, which is itself a measure of how thin the installed base still is. None discloses digital pathology revenue. No revenue market share is publicly disclosed.

recent_developments.event: The whole slide imaging register reached 23 authorisations under product code PSY. The openFDA 510(k) endpoint, queried on 18 October 2026 against a release stamped 5 October 2026, returns four 2026 decisions: Hamamatsu's NanoZoomer S20MD and S360MD (K253606, 15 July), Virasoft's Virasight (K251952, 17 July), Hamamatsu's NanoZoomer S540MD (K260964, 22 July) and Leica Biosystems' Aperio GT 450 DX and GT 180 DX (K253554, 7 August). Across the whole life of the regulation the agency granted 8 authorisations in the seven years 2017 through 2023 and 15 in the under three years since, with 9 of the 23 falling in calendar 2024 alone and none at all in 2018 or 2020.

On 8 October 2026 CMS issued a CLIA proposed rule covering virtual access, gynecologic cytology proficiency testing and personnel qualifications. It would add digital images and digital data to the records laboratories must store under 42 CFR 493.1101(e), revise the retention rules at 493.1105 under which cytology slide preparations are kept at least 5 years and histopathology slides at least 10, permit digital images in gynecologic cytology proficiency testing to align with FDA-authorised digital cytology screening systems, and add qualifications for histopathology gross tissue examination personnel and Mohs dermatology laboratory directors. The rule states laboratory counts from the QCOR system as of 4 August 2025: 248,642 Certificate of Waiver, 16,960 Certificate of Compliance, 16,995 Certificate of Accreditation and 24,441 provider-performed microscopy laboratories, 307,038 in all.

In the same proposed rule CMS priced whole slide imaging per laboratory for the first time in a federal document, estimating that acquiring digital whole slide instrumentation would cost a Certificate of Compliance or Certificate of Accreditation laboratory between $100,000 and $1,500,000 for equipment alone, citing Kumar, Gupta and Gupta in the Journal of Digital Imaging, plus $1,000 to $100,000 for digital software depending on functionality. It also identified 13,582 such laboratories, about 40 percent of the 33,955 total, as hospital-based, independent, industrial, public health or pharmacy laboratories that may already have the capability to use or implement virtual access, and stated plainly that it is unable to determine how many laboratories have adopted digital images for screening as the primary method of patient testing.

In its 29 January 2026 full-year announcement Roche reported Pathology Lab, a Diagnostics Division customer area, at CHF 1,723M for 2025 against CHF 1,599M in 2024, up 14 percent at constant exchange rates and 8 percent in Swiss francs, making it the fastest-growing customer area in a division whose total sales were CHF 13,847M against CHF 14,324M. Core Lab was CHF 7,614M, Molecular Lab CHF 2,527M and Near Patient Care CHF 1,983M. The 2024 comparatives were restated so that Pathology Lab now includes CINtec sales previously reported under Molecular Lab, which means the 14 percent is not comparable with growth rates in earlier Roche reports.

Reported full-year 2025 Diagnostics segment sales of $9,941M and segment operating profit of $2,650M, against $9,787M and $2,625M for 2024, on total company sales of $24,568M. Leica Biosystems Imaging, which holds three of the 23 FDA whole slide imaging authorisations and the only digital pathology image artifact detection clearance, is not reported as a separate line and digital pathology revenue is not disclosed at any level of the segment reporting.

Received DEN240068 on 31 July 2025, the de novo authorisation that created 21 CFR 864.3755 and product code SFH for a pathology software algorithm device analysing digital images for prostate cancer prognosis. It is the third and most recent de novo in the digital pathology family after DEN160056 (Philips, 2017) and DEN200080 (Paige Prostate, 2021). Artera followed it with K254115 for ArteraAI Breast on 4 May 2026 under the companion code SHW, and SimBioSys received K260023 for TumorSight Risk under the same code on 25 September 2026, bringing the prognosis-algorithm class to three authorisations in fourteen months.

Reported Diagnosis & Treatment segment sales of EUR 8,531M for 2025 against EUR 8,790M in 2024, with full-year comparable sales growth of 0 percent, an Adjusted EBITA margin of 11.7 percent for the year and 11.8 percent in the fourth quarter, down 30 basis points mainly due to tariffs, on fourth-quarter comparable sales growth of 4 percent. Philips holds the founding de novo for whole slide imaging and 8 of the 23 authorisations under that regulation, and discloses no IntelliSite Pathology Solution or digital pathology revenue.

regulatory_landscape: 21 CFR 864.3700, the whole slide imaging system regulation created by de novo DEN160056 on 12 April 2017, product code PSY, class II. The FDA's own classification text limits the intended use to an aid to the pathologist in reviewing and interpreting digital images of surgical pathology slides prepared from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue, and states that the system is not intended for use with slides prepared from frozen tissue, cytology, or non-FFPE hematopathology specimens such as peripheral blood smears. Twenty-three authorisations exist under this code

21 CFR 864.3700 as it extends to the rest of the stack: product code QKQ for digital pathology image viewing and management software, 14 authorisations; PZZ for digital pathology displays, 3; and SIX for digital pathology image artifact detection software, 1, granted in August 2026

21 CFR 864.3750, software algorithm device to assist users in digital pathology, product code QPN, created by de novo DEN200080 for Paige Prostate on 21 September 2021 and codified by the FDA's classification rule published on 2 February 2023. Two authorisations exist, the de novo and Ibex Galen Second Read

21 CFR 864.3755, pathology software algorithm device analysing digital images for cancer prognosis, product codes SFH and SHW, created by de novo DEN240068 for ArteraAI Prostate on 31 July 2025. Three authorisations exist, all granted between July 2025 and September 2026

42 CFR part 493, the CLIA laboratory requirements, under which a laboratory performing whole slide imaging for patient testing must hold a Certificate of Compliance or Certificate of Accreditation and meet the high-complexity testing, personnel, quality control and record-retention requirements, including the retention of cytology slide preparations for at least 5 years and histopathology slides for at least 10 years at 493.1105(a)(7)

The CMS CLIA proposed rule of 8 October 2026, which would add digital images and digital data to the records laboratories must maintain under 493.1101(e), create a defined virtual access regime covering transmission of images to a secure off-site location and back, allow digital images in gynecologic cytology proficiency testing in alignment with FDA-authorised digital cytology screening systems, and add personnel qualifications for histopathology gross tissue examination and Mohs dermatology laboratory directors

CPT Category III add-on codes 0751T through 0763T, reported one-to-one with the primary surgical pathology, special stain and immunohistochemistry codes 88302, 88304, 88305, 88307, 88309, 88312, 88313, 88314, 88319, 88341, 88342, 88344 and 88360 when the digitisation procedure of glass microscope slides is performed, and expressly not reportable for archival, educational, AI training or validation, or clinical conference purposes, nor for static photographs or video taken on smartphones or tablets. A further family, 0827T through 0856T, took effect on 1 January 2024

The Medicare Physician Fee Schedule, under which CPT 88305 is paid with a professional and technical component split rather than under the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule. The CY2026 conversion factor is $33.4009 for non-qualifying APM and $33.5675 for qualifying APM, against $32.3465 in CY2025. Neither the CY2023 nor the CY2026 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, nor the CY2026 Hospital Outpatient PPS final rule, contains any mention of the digital pathology add-on codes or of digital pathology at all

research_methodology.data_validation: Six independent divisions were computed against the two public registers that bound this market and cross-checked against each other. The headline division is dollars of published market per laboratory that could install a scanner: $2,010M over the 33,955 non-waived CLIA laboratories CMS counted on 4 August 2025 is $59,196 per laboratory, over the 13,582 CMS itself identifies as digitally capable is $147,990, and over the 3,229 cytology-subspecialty laboratories is $622,484. Against CMS's own stated cost of $100,000 to $1,500,000 for whole slide instrumentation per laboratory, the second of those is 1.48 times the bottom of the range and 0.10 times the top, and that is on the generous reading that gives the whole world's spending to one country's laboratories. Each candidate growth rate was then run through the same denominator: the published CAGR spread of 7.99 percent to 18.56 percent moves the 2032 figure from $3,187.8M to $5,582.5M and the per-laboratory figure from $234,711 to $411,019, a difference of $176,308 a year, or about one mid-range scanner. The decisive division is cumulative. The seven-point series 2026-2032 sums to $19,010.74M at 9.90 percent and $22,244.3M at 15 percent, while equipping the 13,582 candidate laboratories at CMS's $1,500,000 top end costs 13,582 x $1,500,000 = $20,373.0M, which is 1.072 times the first figure and 91.6 percent of the second; at CMS's $100,000 low end it is $1,358.2M, still 67.6 percent of one entire year of the global market. Taking the United States out of the global total at the publishers' own North America shares of 47.8 percent and 39.92 percent gives $9,087.1M and $7,589.1M of cumulative North American spending, or $669,057 and $558,761 per candidate laboratory over seven years against a $800,000 midpoint for one scanner. No published growth rate in this literature therefore funds a complete installed base by 2032, which rules in a partial-adoption reading and rules out the digital-transition framing that accompanies every forecast. Two further divisions bound the market from the supply and vendor sides: there are 13,582 / 23 = 590 candidate laboratories for every whole slide imaging authorisation the FDA has ever granted and 1,358 for every company that holds one; and Roche's disclosed Pathology Lab customer area of CHF 1,723M, which is $2,073.4M at the IRS 2025 average rate of 0.831, is 1.032 times the entire global digital pathology market and 2.904 times the lowest published estimate, which fixes digital pathology as a thin layer on a much larger tissue-diagnostics business rather than as that business. The reimbursement check is an absence rather than a quantity: a Federal Register full-text search run on 18 October 2026 returns zero documents containing 0751T, 0753T or 0763T across the publication's entire history, and the CY2023 and CY2026 Physician Fee Schedule final rules and the CY2026 Outpatient PPS final rule contain no mention of digital pathology at all. None of this is a market estimate. It is a set of plausibility tests against countable registers, and the figures published are a named publisher's own with a one-year extension at that publisher's own stated rate, not ours. One class of figure is deliberately absent: amounts CMS publishes only in its Physician Fee Schedule relative value file, and therefore the dollar payment for CPT 88305, could not be retrieved because every CMS data endpoint returned HTTP 403 to this environment, and they are omitted rather than taken from third-party aggregators.

faqs.question: How big is the digital pathology market, and why do published figures differ so much?
faqs.answer: On the digitisation-stack scope we publish - whole slide imaging scanners, image analysis and AI software, communication and storage systems and slide management, excluding conventional microscopes, generic image archives and outsourced specimen processing - digital pathology is $2,010M in 2026 and reaches $3,541M by 2032 at a 9.90% CAGR. Published 2026 estimates span $714M to $11,818M, a 16.55x range, but the extremes are doing different jobs: the $11,818M figure adds installation, workflow configuration, validation support and maintenance services and is 5.88 times the next highest estimate, while the $714M figure explicitly excludes radiology imaging, non-pathology archives and laboratory information systems without slide capability. Eleven publishers cover the stack itself and they run $714M to $2,010M, a 2.815x spread, with a median of $1,600M.

faqs.question: Does the market disagree about size or about growth?
faqs.answer: Both, by almost exactly the same multiple, which is the unusual thing. Across the eleven estimates that cover the digitisation stack, 2026 sizes are 2.815x apart and CAGRs are 2.323x apart - 7.99% to 18.56% - a ratio of 1.21. In most healthcare markets the sizes disagree by multiples and the growth rates agree, because the publishers are describing different things and calling them one; in a few, such as pharmacovigilance, the reverse holds and the disagreement is purely about forecasting. Digital pathology is neither. There is no dimension along which this literature converges, and the disagreement widens rather than resolving: carried to 2032 on each publisher's own rate the endpoints run $1,534.5M to $4,604.9M, 3.00x apart, and the ordering scrambles, with the publisher holding the third-lowest 2026 base finishing second-highest in 2032.

faqs.question: How many whole slide imaging systems has the FDA actually authorised?
faqs.answer: Twenty-three, under product code PSY and regulation 21 CFR 864.3700, from ten distinct companies, on the openFDA release of 5 October 2026. One is the de novo, DEN160056, granted to Philips on 12 April 2017; the other 22 are 510(k) clearances. Philips holds 8 of the 23, Hamamatsu 4, Leica Biosystems 3 and Roche's Ventana 2, with one each to Barco, Proscia, Sectra, Indica Labs, Shandon Diagnostics and Virasoft. Across the whole digital pathology regulatory family - adding image viewing and management software, displays, artifact detection, assistive algorithms under 864.3750 and prognosis algorithms under 864.3755 - there are 46 authorisations and three de novo classifications in total. The timeline matters more than the total: 8 authorisations in the seven years 2017 through 2023, then 15 in under three years, with 9 of the 23 PSY authorisations falling in calendar 2024 alone and none at all in 2018 or 2020.

faqs.question: Are the digital pathology add-on CPT codes actually paid?
faqs.answer: No, and the evidence is an absence in a searchable register rather than anyone's opinion. The thirteen codes 0751T through 0763T are CPT Category III add-on codes reported one-to-one with the primary surgical pathology, special stain and immunohistochemistry codes. Category III codes carry no relative value units, so there is no national payment amount; whatever is paid is paid at a Medicare Administrative Contractor's discretion with no published rate. A Federal Register full-text search run on 18 October 2026 returns zero documents containing 0751T, 0753T or 0763T across the publication's entire history, and the CY2023 and CY2026 Physician Fee Schedule final rules and the CY2026 Hospital Outpatient PPS final rule contain no occurrence of 0751T, 0753T or the phrase digital pathology. CMS has never assigned these codes a payment amount or discussed them in a fee schedule rule. The College of American Pathologists also states they may not be reported for AI training or validation, which is the fastest-growing use of a digitised slide.

faqs.question: What does the published market work out to per laboratory, and does any forecast fund the installed base?
faqs.answer: It works out to $147,990 per laboratory per year, and no published forecast funds the base. CMS counted 33,955 non-waived CLIA laboratories on 4 August 2025 and identified 13,582 of them - hospital, independent, industrial, public health and pharmacy laboratories - as having the profile to digitise. The entire global market over that second denominator is $147,990, against CMS's own estimate of $100,000 to $1,500,000 to acquire whole slide instrumentation for one laboratory. Run the cumulative test and the gap is unambiguous: the seven-year series 2026-2032 sums to $19,010.74M at our rate and $22,244.3M at 15%, while equipping those 13,582 laboratories at CMS's $1,500,000 top end costs $20,373.0M - 1.072 times the first and 91.6% of the second. Allocate only North America's share, 39.92% to 47.8% on the publishers' own figures, and seven years of spending is $558,761 to $782,857 per candidate laboratory against an $800,000 midpoint for one scanner.

faqs.question: Which vendors lead the digital pathology market, and what are their shares?
faqs.answer: The register answers the first question and nothing answers the second. Philips holds 8 of the 23 whole slide imaging authorisations, Hamamatsu 4, Leica Biosystems 3 and Roche's Ventana 2 - but Philips discloses no IntelliSite revenue inside a Diagnosis & Treatment segment of EUR 8,531M, Danaher reports Diagnostics at $9,941M without breaking out Leica Biosystems, and Hamamatsu publishes no digital pathology line. Proscia, Sectra, Indica Labs, Virasoft, Paige.AI, PathAI, Ibex and Artera are privately held or non-disclosing. Roche is the only participant with a disclosed pathology line, Pathology Lab at CHF 1,723M for 2025, up 14% at constant exchange rates, and that line is anatomic pathology entire rather than digital pathology. Share is not computable from any public document and this report does not estimate it. What can be said is a concentration measure: 590 candidate laboratories for every authorisation ever granted, and 1,358 for every company holding one.

faqs.question: Why does this report publish no regional or country breakdown?
faqs.answer: Because the published splits contradict each other by more than the global totals do in some respects and are irreconcilable within single pages in others. Four publishers give North America's share of a nominally identical market in the same year as 36.74%, 39.92%, 41% and 47.8% - a 1.30x disagreement on one region in one year. Precedence puts North America at $490M and the United States alone at $390M on its own $1.28B global base for 2025, which works out to 38.3% and 30.5% respectively and cannot be reconciled with the 41% the same page states for North America. One of those three numbers is wrong and the page does not say which. The two North America shares are used in the grounding arithmetic to bracket a United States reading and are quoted in prose with their publisher attached, but an omitted section is honest where a fabricated 41% applied to our scope and base year would not be.

faqs.question: Is computational or AI pathology part of this market or a separate one?
faqs.answer: The literature has not decided, and the collision is large enough to change an investment case. Five publishers size computational pathology for 2026 at $715M, $781.5M, $800M, $854M and $1,871M - which overlaps rather than nests inside the $714M to $2,010M range eleven publishers give for the whole digitisation stack. On Grand View Research's own two reports, computational pathology at $781.5M is 48.8% of its $1,600M digital pathology market; and Verified Market Research's entire digital pathology market, $714M, is below three of the five computational-pathology estimates. The FDA register treats them as distinct: scanning and viewing sit under 21 CFR 864.3700, assistive algorithms under 864.3750 with two authorisations, and cancer prognosis algorithms under 864.3755 with three, a regulation that did not exist before July 2025. This report publishes the stack scope and does not sum, difference or ratio the two literatures.

executive_summary: Digital pathology is the digitisation of glass microscope slides and the software that views, stores and reads the resulting whole-slide images, and it is one of the few healthcare IT markets bounded on both sides by countable public registers. On the supply side, the FDA has granted 23 authorisations under product code PSY, the whole slide imaging system regulation at 21 CFR 864.3700, and 46 across the whole digital pathology family, of which three are de novo classifications. On the demand side, CMS counted 33,955 non-waived CLIA laboratories on 4 August 2025 and identified 13,582 of them as having the institutional profile to digitise. Normalised to a common 2026 base, eleven publishers covering the digitisation stack give $714M, $878M, $1,390M, $1,419M, $1,470M, $1,600M, $1,660M, $1,680M, $1,793M, $1,886M and $2,010M - a 2.815x spread - while their growth rates run 7.99%, 8.6%, 9.90%, 10.19%, 12.7%, 13.5%, 13.6%, 13.8%, 16.05%, 18.3% and 18.56%, a 2.323x spread. The ratio of those spreads is 1.21: this literature disagrees about what the market is worth and about how fast it grows by almost exactly the same multiple, and converges on neither. By 2032 the endpoints run $1,534.5M to $4,604.9M, 3.00x apart, and the ordering scrambles. Dividing through the register settles what no forecast here funds. The whole global market over the 13,582 candidate laboratories is $147,990 a year, against CMS's own estimate of $100,000 to $1,500,000 to acquire whole slide instrumentation for one of them. Sum the series and equipping those laboratories at CMS's top end costs $20,373.0M against a cumulative 2026-2032 global market of $19,010.74M - 1.072x - and 91.6% of the $22,244.3M a 15% rate would produce. Allocate only North America's own published share and seven years of spending is $558,761 to $782,857 per candidate laboratory against an $800,000 midpoint for one scanner. Two further divisions bound it. There are 590 candidate laboratories for every whole slide imaging authorisation the FDA has ever granted and 1,358 for every company that holds one, with 8 of the 23 belonging to Philips alone. And Roche's disclosed Pathology Lab customer area, CHF 1,723M for 2025, is $2,073.4M at the IRS yearly average rate - 1.032 times the entire global digital pathology market and 2.904 times its lowest published estimate - which fixes digital pathology as a thin layer on a far larger tissue-diagnostics business rather than as that business. Finally, the reimbursement mechanism cited everywhere as the adoption driver pays nothing: no Federal Register document in the publication's history contains 0751T, 0753T or 0763T, and the CY2023 and CY2026 Physician Fee Schedule final rules and the CY2026 Outpatient PPS final rule do not mention digital pathology at all.
key_highlights: Digital pathology, digitisation-stack scope: $2,010M in 2026 to $3,541.46M in 2032 at 9.90%. The 2032 endpoint is our one-year extension of the publisher's own stated rate, whose horizon ends at $3,210M in 2031.

Published 2026 estimates span $714M to $11,818M - 16.55x - but across three colliding definitions: the digitisation stack at $714M-$2,010M from eleven publishers, computational pathology at $715M-$1,871M from five more, and one services-inclusive figure at $11,818M that is 5.88x the next highest.

Inside the eleven-estimate stack tier, sizes are 2.815x apart and CAGRs 2.323x apart (7.99% to 18.56%), a ratio of 1.21. Unlike most healthcare markets, this literature converges on neither size nor growth.
Carried to 2032 the disagreement widens to $1,534.5M-$4,604.9M, 3.00x, and the ordering scrambles: the publisher with the third-lowest 2026 base finishes second-highest.

Eight of the 23 belong to Philips; 9 of the 23 were granted in calendar 2024 alone against 8 in the whole of 2017-2023.

No published forecast funds the installed base. The cumulative 2026-2032 global market is $19,010.74M at 9.90%, while equipping the 13,582 CLIA laboratories CMS identifies as digital-capable at CMS's own $1,500,000 top end costs $20,373.0M - 1.072x the entire cumulative market, and 91.6% of it even at a 15% rate.
Per laboratory, the whole global market is $147,990 a year against CMS's $100,000-$1,500,000 for one scanner, and the entire 2.32x CAGR disagreement moves that only from $234,711 to $411,019 by 2032.

The add-on CPT codes pay nothing. A Federal Register full-text search on 18 October 2026 returns zero documents containing 0751T, 0753T or 0763T in the publication's entire history, and three successive Medicare fee schedule final rules contain no mention of digital pathology at all.

Roche's disclosed Pathology Lab line of CHF 1,723M for 2025, $2,073.4M at the IRS yearly average rate of 0.831, is 1.032 times the entire global digital pathology market - one company's anatomic pathology customer area is larger than the market nine of eleven publishers describe.
market_context: Digital pathology sits between a device register and a laboratory register, and that is why it can be checked rather than merely cited. The FDA created the category in a single act - de novo DEN160056 on 12 April 2017, which established 21 CFR 864.3700 and product code PSY - and the regulation's own text draws the boundary: an aid to the pathologist in reviewing and interpreting digital images of surgical pathology slides prepared from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue, expressly not frozen sections, cytology or non-FFPE hematopathology. Twenty-three authorisations exist under that code and 46 across the family, three of them de novos, which is the whole regulated universe. The demand side is counted by CMS, and has not moved: non-waived CLIA laboratories were 33,033 on a July 2021 snapshot, 33,747 in the December 2023 fees rule and 33,955 on the August 2025 QCOR pull, of which CMS itself nominates 13,582 as digitally capable. So both terms of the adoption question are public, and the published market divides through them cleanly. What the division shows is that this is a partial-adoption market and not a transition: no growth rate in the literature funds a complete installed base by 2032, and the regulator, which in October 2026 proposed the rules that would make off-site digital review lawful, states in print that it is unable to determine how many laboratories have adopted digital images for primary screening. The commercial structure is equally lopsided. Digitisation attaches to an anatomic pathology business many times its size - Roche alone books CHF 1,723M in its Pathology Lab customer area, which converts to more than the entire global digital pathology market - and the companies holding the authorisations report none of it: Philips holds a third of all whole slide imaging clearances inside a EUR 8,531M segment, Danaher reports Diagnostics at $9,941M without separating Leica Biosystems. Meanwhile the reimbursement mechanism cited in every write-up of this market as its adoption driver has never been assigned a payment amount, never appeared in a fee schedule rule, and may not be reported for the AI use case that is growing fastest.
forecast_analysis: We publish $2,010M for 2026 and $3,541.46M for 2032 at 9.90%, in millions rather than billions, because at this scale a hardcoded billions unit would misstate the market by three orders of magnitude. Two things need saying plainly. First, the scope: this is Mordor Intelligence's definition - solutions that digitise pathology slides and enable viewing, sharing and analysis of whole-slide images, comprising scanners, image analysis and AI software, communication and storage systems, and slide management systems and accessories, with conventional microscopes, generic image archives not tied to pathology workflows and outsourced specimen-processing services excluded. It is chosen not because it is the highest of the eleven normalised estimates, though it is, but because it is one of only two definitions in the whole literature that names its own exclusions, and the other is the extreme low outlier at $714M. Second, the endpoint: Mordor's horizon stops at $3,210M in 2031, so the 2032 figure is our one-year extension of the publisher's own stated rate, not something it publishes. The arithmetic is $2,010M x 1.099^6 = $3,541.4589M, cross-checked against $3,210M x 1.099 = $3,527.79M, a 0.39% difference that is the publisher's own rounding - its stated endpoints imply 9.815%, not the 9.90% it states - and the implied CAGR across 2026-2032 on our series is 9.9000%. The intermediate years are interpolation at a constant rate, not observation, and the chart is labelled as such. The honest statement about the published range is that it is wide in both dimensions at once. Eleven stack-scope 2026 values are 2.815x apart; eleven CAGRs are 2.323x apart; by 2032 the endpoints run $1,534.5M to $4,604.9M, 3.00x apart, and the rank order changes between the two dates. But the more important point is that the choice between those rates is not a choice about whether digital pathology happens. Held against the 13,582 CLIA laboratories CMS identifies as digital-capable, the 7.99% path gives $234,711 per laboratory in 2032 and the 18.56% path gives $411,019 - a difference of $176,308 a year, or roughly one mid-range scanner - and every figure in that range sits in the lower third of CMS's own $100,000 to $1,500,000 cost for one. Cumulatively the series sums to $19,010.74M against $20,373.0M to equip those laboratories at CMS's top end, 1.072x, and taking only North America's own published share of 39.92% to 47.8% leaves $558,761 to $782,857 per laboratory over seven years against an $800,000 midpoint. Whichever rate a reader picks, they are picking a view on how fast a minority of laboratories digitises, not on when pathology becomes digital.
reader_takeaways: Never quote a digital pathology market size without naming which of three definitions it belongs to. The same year supports $714M-$2,010M for the digitisation stack from eleven publishers, $715M-$1,871M for computational pathology from five more, and $11,818M once deployment services are folded in. The gap between the extremes is 16.55x, far larger than any forecast error, and the computational tier overlaps the stack tier rather than nesting inside it.

In this market, interrogate the size and the growth equally. Unlike most healthcare literatures, where one dimension is tight and the other wide, digital pathology's 2026 sizes are 2.815x apart and its CAGRs 2.323x apart - a ratio of 1.21 - and by 2032 the spread widens to 3.00x with the rank order reversed. Taking a base from one house and a rate from another compounds two unrelated disagreements.

Check any digital pathology claim against two exact public counts: 23 FDA whole slide imaging authorisations under 21 CFR 864.3700 from ten companies, and 33,955 non-waived CLIA laboratories of which CMS identifies 13,582 as digital-capable. That is 590 candidate laboratories per authorisation ever granted. Supply-side concentration, not demand, is the structural fact.

Treat the reimbursement driver as unproven until a payment amount exists. The thirteen add-on codes 0751T-0763T have no relative value units, have never appeared in any Federal Register document, are absent from three successive Medicare fee schedule final rules, and may not be reported for AI training or validation. Any adoption case built on them is a case built on contractor discretion with no published rate.

Model this as partial adoption, not a transition. Seven years of global spending at the rate we publish is $19,010.74M, while equipping only the US candidate laboratories at CMS's own high-end instrumentation cost is $20,373.0M. No rate in the literature closes that gap by 2032, and CMS's own assumed digital adoption rate in cytology is 25%.

Treat any vendor share claim here as unverifiable, and do not mistake digital pathology for anatomic pathology. Philips, Danaher, Hamamatsu and every private algorithm vendor disclose no digital pathology revenue; the one disclosed pathology line, Roche's CHF 1,723M Pathology Lab, converts to $2,073.4M - more than the whole published digital pathology market - and it is the business the digitisation layer sits on, not the layer itself.
